The [Lockheed Martin X-33][ref_x33] won its competition, was funded, was very nearly built, and never flew.
It is the exact inverse of the aircraft in the previous article. The [X-32][related_post_a329_boeing_x32]
was built, flew one hundred and forty-four times, and lost.
**The X-33 beat two rivals for the contract, absorbed something over one and a quarter billion dollars, reached a state variously reported as eighty-five percent assembled and ninety-six percent of parts complete, and was cancelled in the early months of 2001 without ever leaving the ground.**
This is the thirty-fourth article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_xplanes_framing], following the
[X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the
[X-3][related_post_a300_douglas_x3], the [X-4][related_post_a301_northrop_x4], the
[X-5][related_post_a302_bell_x5], the [X-6][related_post_a303_convair_x6], the
[X-7][related_post_a304_lockheed_x7], the [X-8][related_post_a305_aerojet_x8], the
[X-9][related_post_a306_bell_x9], the [X-10][related_post_a307_north_american_x10], the
[X-11][related_post_a308_convair_x11], the [X-12][related_post_a309_convair_x12], the
[X-13][related_post_a310_ryan_x13], the [X-14][related_post_a311_bell_x14], the
[X-15][related_post_a312_north_american_x15], the [X-16][related_post_a313_bell_x16], the
[X-17][related_post_a314_lockheed_x17], the [X-18][related_post_a315_hiller_x18], the
[X-19][related_post_a316_curtiss_wright_x19], the [X-20][related_post_a317_boeing_x20], the
[X-21][related_post_a318_northrop_x21], the [X-22][related_post_a319_bell_x22], the
[X-23][related_post_a320_martin_marietta_x23], the [X-24][related_post_a321_martin_marietta_x24], the
[X-25][related_post_a322_bensen_x25], the [X-26][related_post_a323_schweizer_x26], the
[X-27][related_post_a324_lockheed_x27], the [X-28][related_post_a325_osprey_x28], the
[X-29][related_post_a326_grumman_x29], the [X-30][related_post_a327_rockwell_x30], the
[X-31][related_post_a328_rockwell_mbb_x31], and the [X-32][related_post_a329_boeing_x32].

**The programme is remembered for the wrong subsystem.** It is remembered for the linear aerospike engine,
which was exotic and which worked, and for the lifting-body shape, which was unusual and which was
analysable by ordinary means. **What ended it was a tank.** On 3 November 1999, at the National Aeronautics
and Space Administration's [Marshall Space Flight Center][ref_msfc], a graphite-epoxy sandwich tank for
liquid hydrogen completed its structural and cryogenic test programme successfully, was drained, and then
came apart about fifteen minutes later when nothing at all was being done to it.

**This article argues that the failure was not an accident attached to an otherwise sound design, and that the single-point-of-failure reading is the trap the subject sets.**
The tank failed at the end of a chain in which every link is forced by the one before it, and the first link
is the decision to fly home and land on a runway.

## The Research Question

**The keystone is whether the structural mass fraction that [single-stage-to-orbit][ref_ssto] flight demands can be reached, and the X-33 exists to retire the risk on the technologies that would reach it.**

That formulation needs defending, because it is not the one the programme used about itself. The X-33 was
described as a demonstrator of rapid turnaround, of aircraft-like operations, of an advanced engine and an
advanced thermal protection system. All of that is true and none of it is binding.
**A vehicle that turns around quickly and cannot reach orbit is not a launch vehicle.**

### Why the Mass Fraction Is the Binding Unknown

Every other quantity in this programme had a known answer or a bounded one. The aerodynamics of a lifting
body were understood, and this series has already followed that understanding through the
[X-23][related_post_a320_martin_marietta_x23] and the [X-24][related_post_a321_martin_marietta_x24], which
flew and returned data. Rocket engines of the required class existed. Thermal protection for a returning
vehicle had been demonstrated by an operational orbiter for two decades.

**What had never been demonstrated, by anyone, was a reusable vehicle whose empty mass was around a tenth of its fuelled mass.**
The sizing section below shows that the requirement is not a target somebody chose. It falls out of the
rocket equation and the energy of low Earth orbit, and it does not move appreciably for any engine or
trajectory inside the plausible range.

### The Question the Demonstrator Could and Could Not Answer

**Here the article parts company with the previous one in a way that matters.** The X-32 could not answer
its question, because the thing flown was not the thing being bought and the difficulty was one of construct
validity rather than of sampling.
**The X-33's position is the opposite and it is worth stating precisely, because it is the hinge of the whole assessment.**

The X-33 was suborbital. Its own [propellant mass fraction][ref_massfraction] was about seventy-four percent
against the eighty-nine percent an orbital vehicle needs, and **it was never required to close that gap.**
In that respect it could not demonstrate the vehicle-level quantity at all.

**But the tank is different, and the reason is a scaling property rather than an opinion.** For a
thin-walled pressure vessel the structural mass divided by the propellant mass is independent of size. The
derivation is below and the cancellation is exact.
**A subscale tank therefore has the same mass fraction as a full-scale one**, so a demonstrator tank is a
valid test of the tank technology in precisely the dimension that matters. The failure mechanisms are
likewise scale-free. Nothing about cryopumping or about the mismatch of thermal expansion coefficients cares
how large the article is.

**So the X-33 could answer the question it was built to answer, it did answer it, and the answer was no.**
That is a rarer thing in this series than it sounds, and the closing article should record it.

## Programme Origin

### What the Agency Was Trying to Escape

**The context is the cost of getting to orbit and the fact that it had not fallen.** The stated ambition of
the [reusable launch vehicle][ref_rlv] technology programme was a reduction from something on the order of
ten thousand dollars a pound to one thousand, which is a demanded improvement of

$$\frac{10{,}000}{1{,}000} = 10$$

**and the mechanism was to be full reusability** with airline-like operations rather than an expendable
stack rebuilt for every flight.
**An order of magnitude is the kind of target that admits no incremental route**, which is worth holding in
mind against everything that follows.

**The institutional arrangement was unusual and it shaped everything that followed.** The X-33 was not
procured under a conventional contract. It was run as a **cooperative agreement**, in which industry
contributed its own funds and expected to own the resulting commercial vehicle. The
[Government Accountability Office, then the General Accounting Office, reporting on the programme's status in 1999][ref_gao_x33],
put the agency's contribution to the agreement at 912.4 million dollars and the industry partners' estimated
contribution at 286.6 million, the latter having grown by 75 million from an original 211.6 million, which
is

$$\frac{286.6 - 211.6}{211.6} = 0.354$$

**or 35.4 percent, and the growth fell on the industry side rather than the agency's.**

**That structure has a consequence that is easy to miss.** A cooperative agreement in which the contractor
expects to own and operate the product aligns the incentives toward a commercially viable vehicle. It also
means the government's leverage to demand a redesign is weaker than under a procurement, and that the
contractor's willingness to continue depends on a business case that external events can remove.

### The Competition and the Choice

Three teams competed for the Phase II award, and the contract went to [Lockheed Martin's][ref_lockheed]
[Skunk Works][ref_skunkworks] on 2 July 1996. The losing concepts were a vertical-takeoff, vertical-landing
design descended from an earlier flying testbed, and a winged vehicle resembling a scaled-down orbiter with
a cylindrical fuselage and double-delta wings.
**Lockheed Martin's entry was the most technically ambitious of the three on almost every axis**, combining
a lifting body, an untried engine architecture, a metallic thermal protection system and a linerless
composite cryogenic tank.

**A competition that rewards ambition selects for the concept with the most unproven elements**, and this
article's Where the Framing Breaks Down section returns to whether that is a criticism of the selection or
merely a description of what a technology demonstration competition is for.

### The Vehicle It Was For

The X-33 existed to enable **[VentureStar][ref_venturestar]**, a full-scale commercial single-stage-to-orbit
vehicle that Lockheed Martin intended to build and operate. The relationship between the two is quantitative
and it can be checked. VentureStar's published gross mass of 2,184,000 pounds against the X-33's 285,000
gives a mass ratio of

$$\frac{m_{\text{VentureStar}}}{m_{\text{X-33}}} = \frac{2{,}184{,}000}{285{,}000} = 7.663$$

and under a cube law that is a linear scale ratio of

$$\left(7.663\right)^{1/3} = 1.972$$

**which says half scale, from two published masses that were not derived from one another.** The routine
description of the X-33 as a half-scale demonstrator survives an arithmetic check that nobody appears to
have published.

## Sizing From First Principles

### The Requirement Nothing Negotiates

**Let $\Delta v$ be the total ideal velocity increment the vehicle must produce, $I_{sp}$ the trajectory-effective specific impulse, $g_0$ standard gravity, $m_0$ the gross mass and $m_f$ the mass at burnout.**
[The rocket equation][ref_rocketeq] gives, in the form
[Sutton sets out for propulsion analysis][book_rocket_propulsion_elements],

$$\Delta v = I_{sp} \, g_0 \ln\!\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)$$

so the required mass ratio is

$$\frac{m_0}{m_f} = \exp\!\left(\frac{\Delta v}{I_{sp} \, g_0}\right)$$

and the propellant mass fraction $\zeta$, being the share of the gross mass that is propellant, is

$$\zeta = 1 - \frac{m_f}{m_0} = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta v}{I_{sp} \, g_0}\right)$$

**The velocity that has to be produced is mostly, but not only, orbital speed.** A circular orbit of radius
$r$ about a body of gravitational parameter $\mu$ requires that gravity supply exactly the centripetal
acceleration,

$$\frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{\mu}{r^2}$$

so that

$$v_{\text{circ}} = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{r}}$$

**At two hundred kilometres altitude that is**

$$v_{\text{circ}} = \sqrt{\frac{3.986 \times 10^{14}}{6{,}578{,}137}} = 7{,}784.3 \ \text{m/s}$$

**Orbital speed is 7,784.3 metres per second, and the difference between that and the budget is everything the vehicle spends without converting it into orbital speed**,
being gravity losses while the thrust vector is not horizontal, aerodynamic drag through the lower
atmosphere, and the steering that turns one into the other,

$$\Delta v_{\text{losses}} = 9{,}300 - 7{,}784.3 = 1{,}515.7 \ \text{m/s}$$

**The losses come to 1,515.7 metres per second, which is 16.3 percent of the whole budget.** They are not a
rounding allowance. They are a sixth of the requirement, and they are why a launch vehicle cannot be sized
against orbital speed.

**Reaching low Earth orbit therefore costs about 9,300 metres per second, and a hydrogen-oxygen engine delivers a trajectory-effective specific impulse near 430 seconds.**
The effective exhaust velocity is then

$$I_{sp} \, g_0 = 430 \times 9.80665 = 4{,}216.9 \ \text{m/s}$$

the required mass ratio is

$$\frac{m_0}{m_f} = \exp\!\left(\frac{9{,}300}{4{,}216.9}\right) = 9.0742$$

and the propellant fraction is

$$\zeta = 1 - \frac{1}{9.0742} = 0.8898$$

**Eighty-nine percent of the vehicle must be propellant, which leaves 11.02 percent of the gross mass for the structure, the engines, the thermal protection, the tanks, the avionics, the landing gear and the payload together.**

### How Hard That Requirement Is to Move

**A number this demanding invites the hope that a better engine or a cleverer trajectory relaxes it.** The
table below sweeps both across their plausible ranges.

| Specific impulse, seconds | $\Delta v = 9{,}000$ | $\Delta v = 9{,}300$ | $\Delta v = 9{,}600$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 420 | 88.75% | 89.54% | 90.28% |
| 430 | 88.17% | 88.98% | 89.74% |
| 450 | 86.99% | 87.84% | 88.64% |
| 460 | 86.40% | 87.27% | 88.09% |

**Across every combination the requirement stays between 86.4 and 90.3 percent**, so the structural
allowance is between 9.7 and 13.6 percent of gross mass and no choice inside the range escapes it. This is
the same shape of result the [X-30 article][related_post_a327_rockwell_x30] reached for airbreathing ascent,
where a bound that owes nothing to the vehicle turned out to be the most useful thing available, and the
machinery is reused here rather than rebuilt.

**The X-33's own propellant fraction was**

$$\zeta_{\text{X-33}} = \frac{210{,}000}{285{,}000} = 0.7368$$

**or 73.7 percent, which is nowhere near the requirement and was never meant to be.** The demonstrator was
suborbital. What it was required to demonstrate was the technology that would deliver the fraction, and that
is a different kind of test with a different validity argument.

### Hydrogen, Whose Advantage and Whose Penalty Are One Property

**The specific impulse that makes the fraction reachable is available only from hydrogen, and hydrogen is the least dense practical propellant there is.**
[Liquid hydrogen][ref_lh2] at its normal boiling point is 70.85 kilograms per cubic metre against 1,141 for
liquid oxygen, a ratio above sixteen.

**Let $r$ be the mixture ratio, meaning the mass of oxidiser burned per unit mass of fuel.** The fuel and
oxidiser mass fractions of the propellant load are then $1/(1+r)$ and $r/(1+r)$, and the volume occupied per
unit mass of propellant is

$$\frac{V}{m} = \frac{1}{1+r}\frac{1}{\rho_f} + \frac{r}{1+r}\frac{1}{\rho_o}$$

so the bulk density of the combination is the reciprocal,

$$\rho_{\text{bulk}} = \left[\frac{1}{1+r}\frac{1}{\rho_f} + \frac{r}{1+r}\frac{1}{\rho_o}\right]^{-1}$$

**At the mixture ratio of 5.5 that the engine used**, hydrogen is

$$\frac{1}{1+5.5} = 0.154$$

of the propellant mass, and its share of the propellant volume is

$$\frac{(1/6.5)/70.85}{(1/6.5)/70.85 + (5.5/6.5)/1{,}141} = 0.745$$

**Hydrogen is 15.4 percent of the mass and 74.5 percent of the volume.** That single sentence is why this
article is about the hydrogen tank and not about the oxygen tank.

The bulk density of the combination works out at 343.3 kilograms per cubic metre. For kerosene and oxygen at
a mixture ratio of 2.56 the same expression gives 1,023.5, so
**the hydrogen vehicle must find 2.982 times the tank volume for the same propellant mass.** The engine that
makes single-stage-to-orbit arithmetically possible is the engine that makes the tank almost impossible, and
no third option exists, because there is no dense fuel with hydrogen's specific impulse.

### The Ideal Tank, Which Is Reassuring and Irrelevant

**Consider a thin-walled vessel of wall thickness $t$, wall density $\rho_w$, allowable stress $\sigma$, enclosing volume $V$ at internal pressure $p$.**
For a sphere of radius $R$, equilibrium of a hemisphere against the pressure on its projected area gives

$$p \pi R^2 = \sigma \, t \, 2 \pi R$$

so that $t = pR/2\sigma$, and the vessel mass is

$$m = \rho_w \, 4 \pi R^2 t = \frac{2 \pi \rho_w p R^3}{\sigma} = \frac{3}{2} \frac{\rho_w p V}{\sigma}$$

**For a long cylinder the hoop equilibrium of a half shell of length $L$ gives**

$$p \, 2 R L = \sigma \, t \, 2 L$$

so $t = pR/\sigma$, and per unit length

$$m = \rho_w \, 2 \pi R t = \frac{2 \pi \rho_w p R^2}{\sigma} = 2 \frac{\rho_w p V}{\sigma}$$

**So the vessel mass is $k \rho_w p V / \sigma$ with a shape factor $k$ of three halves for a sphere and two for a cylinder, and the size has cancelled.**
Writing $\rho_p$ for the propellant density, the vessel mass divided by the propellant mass it holds is

$$\frac{m_{\text{tank}}}{m_{\text{prop}}} = \frac{k \, \rho_w \, p}{\sigma \, \rho_p}$$

**and this ratio contains no length whatever.**

That cancellation is the reason a demonstrator tank is a valid test. It is also the source of a serious
optimism. Taking a graphite-epoxy laminate of the kind
[Jones treats in the standard text on composite mechanics][book_mechanics_of_composite_materials] at 1,570
kilograms per cubic metre with a design allowable of 450 megapascals, and the protoflight pressure of 42
pounds per square inch, or 289.6 kilopascals, the ideal cylindrical hydrogen tank is

$$\frac{2 \times 1{,}570 \times 289{,}600}{450 \times 10^6 \times 70.85} = 0.02852$$

**or 2.852 percent of the hydrogen it holds.** The same expression for an aluminium-lithium oxygen tank
gives 0.343 percent, so
**the density penalty alone is a factor of 8.32 before any question of shape arises.**

### What the Tank Actually Weighed

Each X-33 hydrogen tank was reported at 4,600 pounds with a capacity of 29,000 United States gallons. That
capacity is 109.78 cubic metres, which holds

$$109.78 \times 70.85 = 7{,}777.7 \ \text{kg}$$

of hydrogen when full, which is 7,777.7 kilograms, against a tank mass of 2,086.5 kilograms.
**The built tank is therefore 26.83 percent of the hydrogen it holds, against an ideal membrane vessel at 2.852 percent, a factor of 9.4.**

**A factor of nine is not a design margin. It is a statement that the tank is sized by something other than the pressure it contains**,
and identifying that something is the rest of this section.

**One comparison sharpens the puzzle before the answer.** The specific strength of the composite is

$$\frac{450 \times 10^6}{1{,}570} = 286.6 \ \text{kN} \cdot \text{m/kg}$$

against

$$\frac{400 \times 10^6}{2{,}700} = 148.1 \ \text{kN} \cdot \text{m/kg}$$

for aluminium-lithium at cryogenic temperature, a ratio of **1.93**. The composite is nearly twice as good
per unit mass.
**And the aluminium-lithium tank that was built to replace the composite one after the failure is reported to have weighed less.**
Whatever the shape and the manufacture cost, they cost more than a factor of two.

### Why the Tank Is Not a Cylinder

**A vehicle that returns from orbit and lands on a runway is a [lifting body][ref_liftingbody] or a winged body, and neither has a circular cross-section.**
A cylindrical tank inside such a vehicle wastes the corners. The alternative is a **conformal** tank, and
the only conformal shape a pressure vessel can take is a set of circular lobes joined along common chords,
because a membrane under uniform pressure must have constant curvature.

**Take a bounding box of width $w$ and height $h$ with $w > h$, and compare two arrangements.** A single
inscribed cylinder has radius $h/2$ and cross-sectional area $\pi h^2/4$. Two equal lobes of the same
radius, placed so their outer extremities touch the sides of the box, have their centres separated by

$$d = w - h$$

and their union area is the sum of two circles less the lens where they overlap,

$$A = 2 \pi R^2 - \left[2 R^2 \arccos\!\left(\frac{d}{2R}\right) - \frac{d}{2}\sqrt{4R^2 - d^2}\right]$$

**For the published X-33 tank envelope of 8.7 by 6.1 by 4.3 metres**, the cross-section of the box is 26.230
square metres, a single inscribed cylinder covers 14.522 of it, or 55.4 percent, and two lobes cover 22.030,
or 84.0 percent. **Lobing raises the volume enclosed in a fixed envelope by a factor of 1.517.**

On a vehicle whose external shape is set by aerodynamics and whose propellant is three quarters hydrogen by
volume, a fifty percent gain in tank volume for the same envelope is not a refinement. It decides whether
the vehicle exists.

### What the Web Costs

**A lobed tank cannot be a bare membrane, because at the junction of two lobes the membrane tensions do not balance.**
Consider the line where two lobes of radius $R$ meet, with centres separated by $d$. Placing the centres at
$(-d/2, 0)$ and $(d/2, 0)$, the lobes intersect at $(0, \pm c)$ with

$$c = \sqrt{R^2 - \left(\frac{d}{2}\right)^2}$$

Each lobe skin carries a membrane tension per unit length of $N = pR$ directed along its own tangent. At the
upper intersection the tangent to the left lobe points along $(-c, d/2)/R$ and the tangent to the right lobe
along $(c, d/2)/R$, so the two skin tensions sum to

$$pR \cdot \frac{(-c, d/2) + (c, d/2)}{R} = (0, \, p\,d)$$

**The skins pull the junction outward along the web with a force per unit length of exactly $p\,d$, so the web must carry**

$$N_{\text{web}} = p \, d$$

**The web tension is the pressure times the separation of the lobe centres, and nothing else enters it.**
The limits confirm the form. As $d \to 0$ the lobes coincide, no web is needed, and the tension vanishes. As
$d \to 2R$ the lobes touch at a point, the web shrinks to nothing, and its tension rises to $2pR$, twice the
hoop tension of either lobe.

For the X-33 envelope, $R$ is 2.15 metres and $d$ is 1.8 metres, so the lobe skin carries 622.6 kilonewtons
per metre and
**the web carries 521.2 kilonewtons per metre, which is 83.7 percent of the hoop load while enclosing no volume at all.**
The web stands 3.905 metres tall.

### The Identity That Says Lobing Is Free

**At this point the natural expectation is that the web is a penalty and that the article is about to price it. It is not a penalty. It is exactly free, and that is a theorem.**

Sizing every wall by its membrane tension, the mass per unit length of the lobed section is the skin arc
length times its thickness plus the web height times its thickness, all times the wall density,

$$m' = \frac{\rho_w p}{\sigma}\left(s R + h_{\text{web}} d\right)$$

where $s$ is the retained arc length of the two lobes and $h_{\text{web}} = 2c$. Writing the half angle
subtended by the removed cap as

$$\alpha = \arccos\frac{d}{2R}$$

the retained arc is

$$s = 2\left(2\pi - 2\alpha\right) R$$

and the union area given above is

$$A = 2\pi R^2 - 2R^2\alpha + \frac{d}{2}\sqrt{4R^2 - d^2}$$

**Substituting and using $h_{\text{web}} = \sqrt{4R^2 - d^2}$,**

$$s R + h_{\text{web}} d = \left(4\pi - 4\alpha\right)R^2 + d\sqrt{4R^2-d^2} = 2A$$

**identically, for every radius and every separation at which the lobes intersect.** The membrane mass per
unit enclosed volume is therefore

$$\frac{m'}{A} = \frac{2 \rho_w p}{\sigma}$$

**which is exactly the value for a cylinder, with the geometry gone.** The residual computed on the X-33
geometry is zero to machine precision, and the identity was tested as a randomised property over twenty
thousand admissible geometries without a single failure.

**A designer who sizes a conformal tank by membrane stress will therefore find that the shape costs nothing, and will be wrong.**
The entire cost of conformality lives in the terms the membrane model does not contain, namely the bending
introduced at every lobe junction, the buckling stability of a wall that must also carry the vehicle's
compressive flight loads, the minimum gauge below which no laminate can be manufactured, and the joints
themselves.

**The membrane model accounts for 10.6 percent of the mass of the tank that was actually built.** The
remaining eighty-nine percent is shape and manufacture, **and the record says exactly that**, because the
reported reason the composite tank came out heavier than the aluminium tank that replaced it was the
complexity of the joints the lobed geometry demanded.

### What the Missing Terms Actually Cost

**An assertion that the cost lives somewhere else is worth very little until the somewhere else is priced.**
This subsection prices the two that can be priced, being buckling and the sandwich the buckling forces, and
reports what remains unaccounted.

#### Buckling, Which Governs

**A thin cylindrical shell in axial compression fails by buckling long before it fails by stress.** The
design practice used here is the agency's own, set out in
[Weingarten, Seide and Peterson's monograph on the buckling of thin-walled circular cylinders][research_viweingarten_pseide_1968],
which is the document that supplies both the knockdown factor below and the pressure-stabilisation term
after it. Writing $E$ for the wall modulus, $\nu$ for its Poisson ratio and $\gamma$ for a knockdown factor
covering imperfection sensitivity, the classical critical stress is

$$\sigma_{cr} = \frac{\gamma E t}{R \sqrt{3\left(1-\nu^2\right)}}$$

so the compressive load per unit circumference the shell can carry is

$$N_{cr} = \sigma_{cr} \, t = \frac{\gamma E t^2}{R \sqrt{3\left(1-\nu^2\right)}}$$

and the thickness stability demands for a given line load $N_x$ is

$$t_{\text{buckling}} = \sqrt{\frac{N_x R \sqrt{3\left(1-\nu^2\right)}}{\gamma E}}$$

**Estimating the X-33's compressive line load would import every uncertainty of its load path, and the argument does not need one.**
Ask instead for the threshold. Setting the buckling thickness equal to the membrane thickness $pR/\sigma$
and solving for the load gives

$$N_x^{\ast} = \frac{\gamma E p^2 R}{\sigma^2 \sqrt{3\left(1-\nu^2\right)}}$$

**Above that line load the wall is sized by stability and not by pressure.** At a knockdown of 0.2, a
laminate modulus of 70 gigapascals and the tank's own radius and pressure, the threshold is

$$N_x^{\ast} = 7.54 \ \text{kN/m}$$

**and the only thing that has to be established about the vehicle is that it clears that bar.** It clears it
easily. Both engines at sea level produce 1.815 meganewtons, and spreading that across the outer contour of
both tanks gives

$$N_x = \frac{1.815 \times 10^6}{2 \times 17.223} = 52.7 \ \text{kN/m}$$

**which is 7.0 times the threshold, from thrust alone**, ignoring inertial loads, aerodynamic bending and
every ground-handling case. The membrane thickness is 1.384 millimetres and the buckling thickness at that
load is

$$t_{\text{buckling}} = 3.656 \ \text{mm}$$

**a ratio of 2.64.** The tank is a stability structure wearing a pressure vessel's name.

**One correction cuts the other way and it belongs here rather than in a footnote.** Internal pressure
stabilises a shell, because hoop tension resists the inward lobes of the buckling mode. The effect scales
with the pressure parameter

$$\frac{p}{E}\left(\frac{R}{t}\right)^2 = 1.430$$

which raises the effective knockdown from 0.2 to 0.429 and drops the required thickness to 2.497
millimetres, **a ratio to the membrane thickness of 1.80 rather than 2.64.**

**The conclusion survives its own correction.** Stability still asks for nearly twice the thickness pressure
asks for, with the tank full and pressurised, **and a tank must also survive being empty.**

| Knockdown factor | Buckling thickness | Ratio to membrane |
|---|---|---|
| 0.10 | 5.171 mm | 3.74 |
| 0.15 | 4.222 mm | 3.05 |
| 0.20 | 3.656 mm | 2.64 |
| 0.30 | 2.985 mm | 2.16 |
| 0.50 | 2.312 mm | 1.67 |
| 1.00 | 1.635 mm | 1.18 |

**Even at a knockdown of one, meaning a shell with no imperfection penalty whatever, buckling asks for 1.635 millimetres against 1.384.**
There is no value of the least certain assumption in this subsection at which pressure governs.

**The critical stress, the knockdown factor and the pressure-stabilisation term are standard results and are not this article's**,
and the literature they come from is a large one.

#### Why That Forces a Sandwich

**A wall that must carry bending as well as membrane load wants its material far from the neutral axis, which is the definition of a [sandwich][ref_sandwich]**,
and the reasoning is the ordinary structural one
[Bruhn sets out for flight vehicle structures][book_analysis_and_design_of_flight_vehicle_st].
**A solid wall thick enough not to buckle is a wasteful way to buy bending stiffness**, because a monocoque
of thickness $t$ has

$$D_{\text{mono}} = \frac{E t^3}{12\left(1-\nu^2\right)} = 313.3 \ \text{N} \cdot \text{m}$$

whereas two facesheets of thickness $t_f$ separated by a core of thickness $h$ have

$$D_{\text{sand}} = \frac{E t_f h^2}{2}$$

**The separation enters squared and the material enters linearly**, which is the whole of the argument for
the architecture. The core thickness that matches the monocoque's stiffness is

$$h = \sqrt{\frac{2 D_{\text{mono}}}{E t_f}} = 2.99 \ \text{mm}$$

**Three millimetres of core buys what three and a half millimetres of solid laminate buys.**

**So the facesheets are not sized by stiffness at all, and what does size them is the finding.** They share
the membrane load, so each needs half the membrane thickness,

$$t_f = \frac{t_{\text{membrane}}}{2} = 0.692 \ \text{mm}$$

against a minimum manufacturable gauge for a balanced symmetric quasi-isotropic laminate of eight plies,

$$t_{\text{gauge}} = 8 \times 0.125 = 1.000 \ \text{mm}$$

**Minimum gauge governs.** The sandwich splits the membrane load between two sheets and thereby pushes each
of them below what can be laid up,
**so material is carried that no load calls for, and no stress calculation will ever object, because nothing is overstressed.**

**A constraint of that kind belongs to manufacture rather than to mechanics, and this article found it to be the thinnest subject it looked for.**
A search of the whole harvested pool for minimum gauge as a design driver returns nothing at all, and the
neighbouring literature on producibility, tolerance and the scale-up of large composite structures is small.
**That is reported rather than padded.** It is also consistent with what the programme itself concluded,
since [the agency's retrospective review][ref_cryotank_review] records that the manufacturing process
revealed complexities in the scale-up of large composite structures that had not been understood before.

#### What the Sandwich Then Weighs

The monocoque wall has an areal mass of

$$\rho_w t_{\text{buckling}} = 1{,}570 \times 0.003656 = 5.740 \ \text{kg/m}^2$$

and the sandwich has

$$2 \rho_w t_f + \rho_c h$$

which depends on a core thickness the record does not give, so it is swept.

**Only the first row of the table below compares equal stiffness**, and that has to be said plainly, because
the rest of it does not. A thicker core buys bending stiffness the monocoque never had, so the last column
is a mass comparison between walls of increasing capability rather than a like-for-like saving.
**A real tank takes the thicker core for reasons this comparison does not price**, namely local buckling of
the facesheets between cells, damage tolerance, handling stiffness and the insulating value of the core
itself.

| Core thickness | Facesheets | Core | Total | Mass against the monocoque | Core share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.99 mm, equal stiffness | 3.14 | 0.19 | 3.33 | 1.72 times lighter | 5.7% |
| 5 mm | 3.14 | 0.32 | 3.46 | 1.66 times lighter | 9.2% |
| 10 mm | 3.14 | 0.64 | 3.78 | 1.52 times lighter | 16.9% |
| 20 mm | 3.14 | 1.28 | 4.42 | 1.30 times lighter | 29.0% |
| 30 mm | 3.14 | 1.92 | 5.06 | 1.13 times lighter | 37.9% |
| 50 mm | 3.14 | 3.20 | 6.34 | 0.91, meaning heavier | 50.5% |

**At equal stiffness the sandwich is 1.72 times lighter and its core is 5.7 percent of the wall.** At a
thirty millimetre core it is only 1.13 times lighter and the core has become 37.9 percent of the wall mass
while carrying no membrane load at all. Setting the sandwich mass equal to the monocoque mass and solving
for the core thickness gives

$$h_{\text{break}} = \frac{\rho_w t_{\text{buckling}} - 2 \rho_w t_f}{\rho_c} = 40.6 \ \text{mm}$$

**Beyond about forty millimetres of core the sandwich weighs more than the solid wall it replaced**, while
being far stiffer than that wall needed to be.

**The saving is real and it is narrower than the architecture's reputation suggests, and the reason is the minimum gauge above.**
A sandwich whose facesheets cannot be made thin enough to exploit the separation is paying for two skins and
a core to do the work that one skin and a thin core would do.
**The architecture is right and it is not free**, and the part of it that is not free is the part that ends
this article.

**The failure mode a sandwich is normally checked against is not the one that occurred**, and it is worth
showing that it was not close. Face wrinkling, the local instability of a facesheet on an elastic
foundation, occurs near

$$\sigma_{wr} = 0.5 \left(E_f E_c G_c\right)^{1/3} = 559.3 \ \text{MPa}$$

against a laminate allowable of 450, **a margin of 1.24.** The tank did not fail in any mode the stress
analysis owned.

**The sandwich bending stiffness, the wrinkling correlation and the minimum-gauge argument are likewise standard**,
and belong to the sandwich structures literature rather than to this article.

#### The Mass That Is Still Unaccounted

**Summing the wall over the tank's surface gives a build-up that can be checked against the article that was built.**
Taking the barrel skin over the outer contour, the web over its own height, and end closures at 1.4 times
the flat cross-section, the sheet area of one tank is

$$s \, L + h_{\text{web}} L + 2 \times 1.4 \, A = 245.50 \ \text{m}^2$$

and at the thirty millimetre sandwich the wall mass is

$$5.06 \times 245.50 = 1{,}242.2 \ \text{kg}$$

**The wall comes to 1,242.2 kilograms against a built tank of 2,086.5, so the build-up explains 59.5 percent and leaves 844.3 kilograms unaccounted.**

**The shortfall is the result rather than a failure of the build-up.** What is missing is exactly the list
the identity pointed at and this article has not costed, namely the joints between the three major
subassemblies, the longerons, the local reinforcement at every penetration and fitting, and the doublers a
lobe junction needs to carry bending into its web.

**That last term is not an unstudied one, and it is worth naming the literature this article declines to reproduce.**
The stress field at the junction of intersecting shells was worked out for multicellular structures in the
1960s, in a report series on
[juncture stress fields in multicellular shell structures][research_almrothbo_broganfa_1965] that runs to at
least eight volumes and includes
[the buckling analysis of the junction itself][research_almrothbo_pittnerev_1965], and a
[two-hundred-inch multicell tank was pressure tested][research_burnettemf_sturmrg_1968] in 1968.
**The knowledge that a lobed tank is expensive at its junctions was thirty years old when the X-33 was designed**,
which makes the membrane model's silence a choice of model rather than an absence of information.
**The membrane model saw none of it. This build-up sees a little over half of what the membrane model missed, and the remainder is the shape.**

**Four relations in this section are constructions of this article rather than citable results, and saying which is better than citing something adjacent and calling it attribution.**
They are the web tension as pressure times the separation of the lobe centres, the identity that the
retained arc times the radius plus the web height times the separation equals twice the enclosed area, the
inversion of that geometry for the line load at which stability overtakes pressure, and the mass build-up
against the article that was built.
**The first two are elementary once written down, the third is arithmetic on the first, and the fourth is bookkeeping.**
None of them is novel physics and none of them has a source, because none of them needs one.

**And a sandwich has a core, and the core is a cellular void, and on this tank it was unvented.** That is
the last link in the chain. Buckling forced the sandwich, the sandwich brought the core, and the core is
what sat against liquid hydrogen at twenty kelvin and was then allowed to warm up.
**The section on what an unvented core does is the end of an argument that begins with the decision to land on a runway.**

## The Vehicle

**The X-33 was a wingless lifting body with two canted vertical fins, two body flaps, a metallic thermal protection system and two linear aerospike engines at the base.**
It was to be launched vertically from a purpose-built site at Edwards Air Force Base and to land
horizontally on a conventional runway, with fifteen suborbital flights planned to landing sites in Utah and
Montana.

The published figures, with the caveat about their disagreement noted below, are a gross mass of 285,000
pounds carrying 210,000 pounds of propellant, a length near 69 feet and a span near 77 feet.

### The Specifications Disagree, and the Disagreement Is a Datum

**Two families of published specification exist and they do not match.** One gives a gross mass of 285,000
pounds and a propellant load of 210,000, so a burnout mass of 75,000. Another gives a gross mass of 272,900
pounds and an unfuelled mass of 63,000, so a propellant load of 209,900.

**The propellant load agrees to within a tenth of a percent and the empty mass differs by 12,000 pounds, which is nineteen percent of the smaller figure.**
The genre convention of this series is to name a disagreement rather than resolve it silently, and here the
disagreement is informative. Neither table is wrong.
**They are two snapshots of a vehicle that was getting heavier**, and the Flight Test Record section derives
the same growth by a third route that uses neither figure.

### A Specification Error Worth Naming

**Widely copied specification tables give the X-33's thrust as 410,000 pounds force per engine.** The
[XRS-2200][ref_xrs2200] was rated at 204,000 pounds force at sea level, and the vehicle had two of them, for
a total of 408,000. **The table has taken the two-engine total and labelled it as the per-engine figure.**

The consequence is arithmetically visible. The correct thrust-to-weight ratio at liftoff is

$$\frac{2 \times 204{,}000}{285{,}000} = 1.432$$

which is ordinary for a launch vehicle. Taken at face value the table implies

$$\frac{2 \times 410{,}000}{285{,}000} = 2.877$$

**which no launch vehicle has ever had, because the propellant would be gone before the vehicle had turned downrange.**
A liftoff ratio near 1.4 is the design region for a hydrogen vehicle, whose engines are heavy and whose
gravity losses are tolerated in exchange for specific impulse.

## Dependent Systems

### The Hydrogen Tanks

**The two liquid hydrogen tanks were the primary structure, not tankage carried inside a structure.** Each
measured 8.7 by 6.1 by 4.3 metres overall, held 29,000 United States gallons, and weighed 4,600 pounds. Each
was a multi-lobed, linerless graphite-epoxy sandwich with an inner facesheet, an **unvented** graphite-epoxy
honeycomb core and an outer facesheet, with integrally bonded woven composite joints, built in three major
subassemblies comprising a forward dome and bulkhead, a barrel section and an aft dome and bulkhead. Those
details, and much of what follows about the failure, are set out in
[the agency's review of the state of the art in liquid hydrogen cryogenic tank structures][ref_cryotank_review].

**Two of those adjectives are the article's subject.** Linerless means there is no metallic foil between the
hydrogen and the laminate, so the laminate itself is the pressure boundary and the permeation barrier.
**Load-bearing means the tank is the airframe**, so its walls carry the vehicle's compressive and bending
flight loads as well as the internal pressure, which is what drives the wall to a sandwich and the core to a
substantial thickness.

The tanks together weigh 9,200 pounds against a burnout mass of 75,000, so

$$\frac{9{,}200}{75{,}000} = 0.1227$$

**One subsystem holding one seventh of the propellant by mass accounts for 12.27 percent of everything the vehicle has left at burnout.**

### Why the Inner Facesheet Was Certain to Crack

**A carbon-fibre epoxy laminate taken to twenty kelvin cracks, and the arithmetic that says so is short.** A
unidirectional ply has a longitudinal expansion coefficient near $-0.4 \times 10^{-6}$ per kelvin, dominated
by the fibre, and a transverse coefficient near $30 \times 10^{-6}$ per kelvin, dominated by the matrix.
**In a laminate, a ply is prevented from contracting transversely by the fibres of its neighbours**, so the
mismatch appears as transverse tensile strain.

Writing $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ for the two coefficients and $\Delta T$ for the excursion from the cure
temperature, the constrained transverse strain is

$$\varepsilon_2 = \left(\alpha_2 - \alpha_1\right)\left|\Delta T\right|$$

**From a cure temperature of about 450 kelvin down to liquid hydrogen at 20.3 kelvin the excursion is 429.7 kelvin**,
and with a mismatch of $30.4 \times 10^{-6}$ per kelvin,

$$\varepsilon_2 = 30.4 \times 10^{-6} \times 429.7 = 0.01306$$

**or 1.306 percent.** The implied transverse stress, at a transverse modulus near 9 gigapascals, is

$$\sigma_2 = 9 \times 10^{9} \times 0.01306 = 117.6 \ \text{MPa}$$

**The transverse failure strain of such a laminate is matrix-dominated and near 0.6 percent**, so the
cooldown alone takes the material to

$$\frac{0.01306}{0.006} = 2.18$$

**times its transverse failure strain before any pressure is applied at all.**

**Microcracking of an epoxy laminate at twenty kelvin is therefore not a workmanship question.** It is what
the numbers require. The only genuinely open question was whether the cracks would link into a connected
leak path through the facesheet, and the failure investigation found that they did.

**Inverting the relation shows why there was no easy fix.** The cure temperature that would hold the strain
inside the allowable is

$$T_{\text{cure}} = 20.3 + \frac{0.006}{30.4 \times 10^{-6}} = 217.7 \ \text{K}$$

**or about minus 55 degrees Celsius.** No structural epoxy cures below room temperature and retains its
properties, so the remedy is not a process change. It is a different resin system, a thin foil barrier, or a
design that tolerates a cracked laminate.

### What an Unvented Core Does

**There are two independent routes to a core pressure large enough to peel a facesheet off, and both are one line of algebra.**

**The first requires no condensation at all.** Gas sealed into a cell at one atmosphere while the cell is at
hydrogen temperature obeys, at constant volume,

$$\frac{p_2}{p_1} = \frac{T_2}{T_1}$$

so warming from 20.3 kelvin to 300 gives a pressure ratio of

$$\frac{300}{20.3} = 14.78$$

**and a core pressure of 1,497 kilopascals, or about 217 pounds per square inch.** A sealed void adjacent to
liquid hydrogen is a pressure vessel whose charging mechanism is being left alone to warm up.

**The second route is [cryopumping][ref_cryopumping], and it is worse.** Nitrogen purge gas that reaches the
cold inner facesheet condenses and then freezes, which lowers the pressure in the cell and draws in more
gas, which condenses in turn. **The process is self-sustaining for as long as the cold surface is cold.**
When the tank is emptied and the wall warms, the accumulated condensate returns to gas in a fixed volume.

Let $f$ be the fraction of the core volume occupied by condensate of density $\rho_c$ and molar mass $M$. On
evaporation into the same volume at temperature $T$ the pressure is

$$p = \frac{f \rho_c R T}{M}$$

so the fill fraction needed to reach a given pressure is

$$f = \frac{p M}{\rho_c R T}$$

**The table below takes solid nitrogen at 1,026 kilograms per cubic metre, warming to 300 kelvin.**

| Bond strength to be exceeded | Core fill fraction required |
|---|---|
| 100 pounds per square inch | 0.755% |
| 200 pounds per square inch | 1.509% |
| 400 pounds per square inch | 3.019% |
| 700 pounds per square inch | 5.283% |

**At a degraded flatwise bond of 200 pounds per square inch, 1.509 percent of the core volume is enough.**
Fifteen parts in a thousand. The investigation reported the bondline strength and toughness as reduced,
**which moves the threshold down rather than up.**

**The same arithmetic for hydrogen, which is what the microcracks actually admitted**, needs a hydrogen
density of 1.1144 kilograms per cubic metre for 200 pounds per square inch at room temperature, which is a
core fraction of 1.573 percent of the density of the liquid.

**The purge that supplied the condensate is not incidental, and it is worth saying where it comes from.** A
cryogenic tank in air will condense and then freeze atmospheric oxygen and nitrogen on any surface it cools,
so the cavity around it is filled with dry nitrogen to keep air out.
**The purge exists because the tank is cold and insulated**, and the insulation system, the purge and the
sealed core are three parts of one arrangement rather than three independent choices.

**The heat leak that makes all of it necessary follows from the same geometry that made the tank hard.** A
tank sized by volume rather than by mass has a large surface area for the propellant it holds, and
hydrogen's low density is what makes the area large, so
**the propellant that is hardest to contain is also the one with the most surface through which to boil away.**

### The Aerospike Engine, Which Worked

**The XRS-2200 [linear aerospike][ref_aerospike] is the part of the programme that is remembered and it is not the part that failed.**
Two engines, each rated at 204,000 pounds force at sea level and 266,000 in vacuum, with a specific impulse
of 339 seconds at sea level and 439 in vacuum, a chamber pressure of 840 pounds per square inch and an
equivalent area ratio of 58.

**The case for altitude compensation is quantitative and this section makes it.** Thrust is the momentum
flux of the exhaust plus a pressure term acting over the exit area,

$$F = \dot{m} v_e + \left(p_e - p_a\right) A_e$$

**and the second term is the whole of the altitude problem**, because it is the only part that depends on
where the engine is. Normalising by chamber pressure and throat area gives the thrust coefficient,

$$C_F = \frac{F}{p_c A_t}$$

while everything upstream of the throat collects into the characteristic velocity,

$$c^{\ast} = \frac{p_c A_t}{\dot{m}}$$

so that specific impulse factors into a chamber term and a nozzle term,

$$I_{sp} = \frac{F}{\dot{m} g_0} = \frac{C_F \, c^{\ast}}{g_0}$$

**That factorisation is why the comparison below can be made in thrust coefficients alone.** For one engine
compared against itself at two ambient pressures the chamber is unchanged, so $c^{\ast}$ cancels exactly and

$$\frac{I_{sp,\text{vac}}}{I_{sp,\text{SL}}} = \frac{C_{F,\text{vac}}}{C_{F,\text{SL}}}$$

A conventional bell nozzle has a fixed exit area, so its exit pressure is fixed by the chamber conditions
and it is correctly expanded at exactly one altitude.
**Let $p_c$ be chamber pressure, $p_e$ exit pressure, $p_a$ ambient pressure, $\varepsilon$ the area ratio and $\gamma$ the ratio of specific heats.**
The area ratio follows from the isentropic relations as

$$\varepsilon = \frac{\left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^{\frac{1}{\gamma-1}} \left(\frac{p_e}{p_c}\right)^{-\frac{1}{\gamma}}}{\sqrt{\frac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}\left[1 - \left(\frac{p_e}{p_c}\right)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}}\right]}}$$

and the thrust coefficient is

$$C_F = \sqrt{\frac{2\gamma^2}{\gamma-1}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^{\frac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}}\left[1 - \left(\frac{p_e}{p_c}\right)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}}\right]} + \left(\frac{p_e}{p_c} - \frac{p_a}{p_c}\right)\varepsilon$$

**The relation is checked against the condition that defines the throat**, namely that the area ratio must
equal one exactly at the critical pressure ratio, and it does so to machine precision.

**At an area ratio of 58 and a chamber pressure of 840 pounds per square inch, the exit pressure is 7.552 kilopascals**,
which is 0.0745 of sea-level ambient. The usual criterion for attached flow puts the separation limit near

$$p_e \geq 0.4 \, p_a$$

which at sea level is 40.53 kilopascals, so the nozzle sits

$$\frac{0.4 \times 101{,}325}{7{,}552} = 5.37$$

**times inside the separation region, and a fixed bell of this area ratio could not be run at sea level at all.**

The comparison that matters takes three nozzles on the same chamber.

| Nozzle | Area ratio | Thrust coefficient at sea level | Thrust coefficient in vacuum |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bell matched at sea level | 7.79 | 1.5734 | 1.7096 |
| Bell at the quoted area ratio | 58.00 | 0.8991 | 1.9138 |
| Altitude compensating | 58.00 | 1.5734 | 1.9138 |

**The compensating nozzle takes the sea-level column from the small nozzle and the vacuum column from the large one**,
which is the entire claim made for the architecture, and the claim is true.

**The published specific impulses provide a check on the specification rather than on the engine.** Their
ratio is

$$\frac{439}{339} = 1.2950$$

against 1.2164 for an ideal compensating nozzle, a disagreement of 6.07 percent, which is what one expects
once real losses and a varying ratio of specific heats are admitted.
**A fixed bell of the quoted area ratio would give a ratio of 2.129**, which is nothing like the published
pair. The published numbers therefore discriminate strongly, and they identify the engine as a compensating
one.

Sweeping the one assumed quantity confirms that the conclusion does not rest on it.

| Ratio of specific heats | Computed specific impulse ratio |
|---|---|
| 1.18 | 1.2237 |
| 1.20 | 1.2164 |
| 1.22 | 1.2093 |
| 1.24 | 1.2025 |

### Thermal Protection

**The X-33 used a metallic thermal protection system rather than [the ceramic tiles of the operational orbiter][ref_tps]**,
on the argument that metal panels are more durable, more tolerant of handling and rain, and faster to
inspect and replace, all of which serve the operations goal rather than the mass goal.

**This is a subsystem chosen for turnaround rather than for weight, and that is worth flagging**, because
the mass budget derived above leaves very little room for a subsystem that is heavier than the alternative.
The Where the Framing Breaks Down section returns to the tension between the operability goals and the mass
fraction requirement, which pull in opposite directions more often than the programme's own statements
acknowledge.

### Aerodynamics and Flight Control

**The lifting-body shape follows from the requirement to return and land horizontally without the mass of a wing.**
The aerodynamic work was conventional in method, resting on wind tunnel testing across the speed range and
on computational prediction, with an entry problem of the class
[Chou treats for reusable launch vehicle trajectories][book_near_optimal_re_entry_trajectories_for_r], and
the series has already covered the lifting-body lineage in the articles on the
[X-23][related_post_a320_martin_marietta_x23] and the [X-24][related_post_a321_martin_marietta_x24].

The operations concept, of the kind
[Rampino examined for a reusable launch vehicle][book_concepts_of_operations_for_a_reusable_la], depended on
it. **The vehicle was to be unpiloted and autonomous**, which removes an entire class of difficulty this
series has met repeatedly, namely the handling qualities of a vehicle a human must fly, and replaces it with
the requirement that the guidance and control system be right the first time.

### The Metallic Tanks, Which Are the Comparison

**The liquid oxygen tank was aluminium rather than composite, and the reason is documented and is not what one would guess.**
The Government Accountability Office records that schedule constraints early in the programme led Lockheed
Martin to exercise an option under the cooperative agreement to use an aluminium oxygen tank, and that an
operational VentureStar would still require a composite oxygen tank to reach its weight.

**So the programme had already conceded one composite tank to schedule before the other one failed**, and it
planned to demonstrate the deferred technology on a ten-foot-diameter ground test article instead.

**After the failure the hydrogen tank was to be replaced with [aluminium-lithium][ref_alli] as well.** The
reported outcome of that decision is the sharpest fact in the article, and it is reported here with its
provenance rather than asserted, because the sources for it are secondary.
**The replacement aluminium-lithium tank is reported to have weighed less than the composite tank it replaced, with the complexity of the joints demanded by the lobed shape cited as the reason.**

If that report is accurate, then the entire rationale for the composite tank had evaporated, and it had
evaporated for a reason that the identity derived above predicts.
**The membrane model says the shape is free. The shape was not free. The difference is the joints.**

**The metal tank does not get the trade for nothing, and the quantity that decides it is the same one that cracks the laminate.**
A tank of length $L$ contracts on filling by

$$\Delta L = \alpha \, \Delta T \, L$$

and over the tank's 8.7 metres, cooling from room temperature to liquid hydrogen, the two materials differ
by more than an order of magnitude.

| Material | Expansion coefficient | Contraction over 8.7 metres |
|---|---|---|
| Graphite epoxy | $2 \times 10^{-6}$ per kelvin | 4.74 mm |
| Aluminium | $23 \times 10^{-6}$ per kelvin | 54.57 mm |

**The ratio is 11.5.** An aluminium tank moves more than five centimetres relative to everything mounted on
it, which the attachments, the thermal protection and every line crossing the boundary must absorb.

**So the property that makes the composite crack is the property that makes it stay still.** A near-zero
expansion coefficient is why the fibres will not let the matrix contract, which is the microcracking derived
above, **and it is also why the tank barely moves.** The metal tank does not solve the problem. It exchanges
an internal problem for an external one.

## The Flight Test Record

**There is none. The X-33 never flew.** That sentence is the flight test record, and the section exists to
say what was tested instead, because a great deal was.

### What Was Actually Tested

The two aerospike engines were assembled and hot-fired on the ground. The liquid oxygen tank completed its
structural test programme. The metallic thermal protection panels were tested, including on a flying
testbed. The hydrogen tank completed its cryogenic and structural loads programme at Marshall Space Flight
Center and then failed after that programme was complete.

**The vehicle itself reached a state reported as eighty-five percent assembled with ninety-six percent of its parts delivered**,
and the launch site at Edwards Air Force Base was built.

### The Test That Ended It

**The sequence on 3 November 1999 is documented and it matters.** The article had completed a protoflight
programme that included pressurisation with liquid nitrogen at 32 pounds per square inch at thirty percent
full and with liquid hydrogen at 42 pounds per square inch at full capacity, with external loads applied to
simulate pre-takeoff, takeoff, ascent, return and landing. **The test was completed successfully.** The tank
was drained and a purge began. About fifteen minutes later the outer facesheet and the core of one lobe
separated from the inner facesheet, the separation initiating in the acreage of that lobe and being, in the
investigation's word, instantaneous.

**The investigation ran from mid-November 1999 to early February 2000 and listed a combination of causes**,
namely microcracking of the inner facesheet with subsequent hydrogen infiltration, cryopumping of the
exterior nitrogen purge gas, higher than expected core pressures, reduced bondline strength and toughness,
and manufacturing flaws. The findings were reported by [Niedermeyer and Munafo][ref_tank_findings] and in
[the investigation's own summary of findings][research_niedermeyermindy_clintonrgjr_2000].

**Two observations about that list are this article's own.** The first is that the five causes are not
independent and are not equally fundamental. **Microcracking is thermodynamically forced**, as the
arithmetic above shows, and the core pressure follows from it with no further assumption. The manufacturing
flaws are the only item on the list that better workmanship would have removed, and they are last.
**The second is that the test procedures and parameters were found to have been within the design limits of the article**,
which means the tank failed under conditions it was designed to survive.

### The Speed Objective, Which Is a Weight Report

**The flight test programme was reduced before it began, and the reduction is quantifiable.** The Government
Accountability Office records that the maximum flight-test speed objective was cut from Mach 15 to Mach 13.8
because the detailed design phase determined that the vehicle's projected weight would exceed requirements
and prevent it from reaching the higher speed. **It says no more than that.** The rocket equation converts
the sentence into a number.

**The published Mach figures are referenced to the sea-level standard speed of sound of 340.294 metres per second**,
which can be checked against the quoted equivalence of Mach 13 to 9,896 miles per hour. The velocity given
up is

$$\Delta v_{\text{lost}} = \left(15.0 - 13.8\right) \times 340.294 = 408.4 \ \text{m/s}$$

Holding the gross mass fixed, the burnout mass that would have reached the original objective satisfies

$$m_f^{\ast} = \frac{m_f}{\exp\!\left(\Delta v_{\text{lost}} / I_{sp} g_0\right)}$$

and the implied growth is $m_f/m_f^{\ast} - 1$.

| Effective specific impulse, seconds | Burnout mass that reaches Mach 15 | Growth |
|---|---|---|
| 350 | 66,587 lb | 12.6% |
| 380 | 67,216 lb | 11.6% |
| 400 | 67,585 lb | 11.0% |
| 439 | 68,213 lb | 9.9% |

**Across every plausible effective specific impulse the implied growth in burnout mass is between 9.9 and 12.6 percent**,
and the inversion is checked forward by putting each inverted mass back through the rocket equation and
confirming that the missing velocity reappears.

**An independent route through the published specification tables lands in the same region.** The difference
between the earlier unfuelled mass of 63,000 pounds and the later gross-minus-propellant figure of 75,000 is
19.0 percent. The two routes share no input.
**One uses a speed objective and an engine, the other uses two mass tables, and neither uses a weight figure the programme withheld.**

## Comparison With Ground Prediction

**This section normally compares what was predicted with what was measured in flight. Here there is no flight, so the comparison is between what was predicted and what the ground test found**,
which turns out to be a more interesting exercise than usual.

### Where Prediction and Test Agreed

**The engine performed.** The XRS-2200 was hot-fired and the published specific impulses are internally
consistent with an altitude-compensating nozzle, as the check above shows.
**The oxygen tank passed its structural programme.** The thermal protection panels were tested and survived.
**The aerodynamic work was conventional and there is no indication in the record that it produced surprises**,
which is unsurprising in turn, because a lifting body at these conditions is a shape the discipline had been
characterising since the 1960s.

### Where Prediction and Test Disagreed

**The hydrogen tank passed every test it was designed for and then failed with no load applied.** That is a
peculiar kind of disagreement, and it is worth being precise about its nature.
**The structural prediction was not wrong.** The tank carried the pressures and the simulated flight loads
it was built to carry. **The prediction that was wrong was a prediction nobody had made**, because the
failure mode was not in the analysis at all.

**This is the most instructive thing in the programme.** The models used were models of a structure under
load. The failure was thermodynamic and it acted through a mechanism, the sealed cellular core, whose
behaviour is not part of a structural analysis.
**The item that killed the vehicle was not mispredicted. It was unmodelled.**

**The second disagreement is the mass, and it was visible years before the test.** The reduction of the
speed objective from Mach 15 to Mach 13.8 during detailed design is a dated, published admission that the
predicted mass had been exceeded, and the inversion above puts the exceedance between about ten and thirteen
percent of burnout mass.

### The Comparison That Was Never Made

**The X-33 was to be compared against VentureStar's requirements, and that comparison can be made now without it ever having flown**,
because it depends on masses rather than on flight data. The next section does it.

## What the Data Changed

### The Verdict, Which Does Not Depend on the Failure

**Take the tank efficiency the programme demonstrated, apply it to the vehicle the demonstration existed to enable, and ask what share of that vehicle's structural allowance the hydrogen tanks would consume.**

VentureStar's published gross mass is 2,184,000 pounds. At the required propellant fraction of 0.8898
derived above, the propellant load is 1,943,317 pounds. Assuming a payload of 45,000 pounds to low Earth
orbit, **everything else, meaning the entire vehicle, has an allowance of**

$$2{,}184{,}000 - 1{,}943{,}317 - 45{,}000 = 195{,}683 \ \text{lb}$$

At a mixture ratio of 5.5 the hydrogen load is 298,972 pounds.
**At the X-33's demonstrated tank efficiency of 26.83 percent of the hydrogen held, the hydrogen tanks alone would weigh**

$$0.2683 \times 298{,}972 = 80{,}205 \ \text{lb}$$

which as a share of the allowance is

$$\frac{80{,}205}{195{,}683} = 0.410$$

**or 41.0 percent of the entire structural allowance for the whole vehicle.** The allowance is 195,683
pounds and the two hydrogen tanks account for 80,205 of it.

**Forty-one percent, for the tanks alone.** The engines, the oxygen tank, the thermal protection, the
airframe, the landing gear, the avionics, the actuators and the plumbing must fit in the remaining
fifty-nine.

**At the ideal membrane efficiency of 2.85 percent the same tanks would be 8,527 pounds, or 4.4 percent of the allowance**,
which is comfortable. The distance between 4.4 and 41.0 is the entire technical content of the programme.

**Inverting the question gives the requirement.** Allowing the tanks a share $f$ of the structural allowance
$m_{\text{dry}}$, the efficiency they must reach against a hydrogen load $m_{H_2}$ is

$$\eta = \frac{f \, m_{\text{dry}}}{m_{H_2}}$$

and the improvement demanded over what was demonstrated is $\eta_{\text{X-33}} / \eta$. At fifteen percent
of the allowance,

$$\eta = \frac{0.15 \times 195{,}683}{298{,}972} = 0.0982$$

$$\frac{0.2683}{0.0982} = 2.73$$

| Share of the structural allowance | Required tank efficiency | Improvement over the X-33 tank |
|---|---|---|
| 10% | 6.5% | 4.10 times |
| 15% | 9.8% | 2.73 times |
| 20% | 13.1% | 2.05 times |
| 25% | 16.4% | 1.64 times |

**Even at a generous fifteen percent of the entire allowance, the tanks must reach 9.8 percent of the hydrogen they hold, which is 2.73 times better than the article that was built and tested.**

**This is the verdict and it owes nothing whatever to the failure.** Had the tank passed its test on 3
November 1999 and every test after it, the arithmetic above would be unchanged, because it uses the tank's
mass and not its integrity.
**The demonstrator demonstrated something, and what it demonstrated was a number that does not close.**

### What the Programme Settled

**It settled that a linerless composite sandwich cryogenic tank of that generation was not a solution**, and
it settled it in a way that was expensive and unambiguous. The subsequent literature treats the X-33 tank as
the reference case for the problem, and the programme is recorded in
[the agency's own history of the X-vehicles][ref_xvehicles], and the specific lessons, namely that matrix
microcracking must be designed against rather than assumed away, that permeation barriers may be necessary
after all, and that cores must be vented, are visible in the work that followed.

**It settled that altitude compensation works and can be built.** The engine is the part of the programme
that did what it said.

**It did not settle whether single-stage-to-orbit is achievable**, and the honest reading is that it did not
get close enough to the question to settle it. What it produced was one strong piece of negative evidence
about one route to the mass fraction.

### What It Fed Into

**The composite cryotank line of work did not stop, and that is the most important thing to say about the aftermath.**
Subsequent programmes pursued the same objective with the X-33's lessons folded in, using barrier films,
vented cores, toughened resin systems and out-of-autoclave processes.
**The largest composite cryogenic tanks built since are considerably larger than the X-33's and did not fail in the same way.**

**What did not survive was the vehicle concept.** The decision history of the vehicle it was meant to
succeed is set out in [Heppenheimer's account of the shuttle decision][book_the_space_shuttle_decision]. The
reduction of launch cost that the programme was chartered to pursue did eventually arrive, and it arrived
from a direction the programme did not consider, namely partial reusability of a two-stage vehicle with
propulsive recovery of the first stage. **The single-stage-to-orbit route remains unflown.**

**That is worth stating plainly rather than triumphally.** Two-stage recovery does not prove that
single-stage-to-orbit is impossible. It proves that a different route reached the goal first, and the
difference between those two statements is the difference between engineering and hindsight.



### What It Failed to Influence

**The programme's operability objectives left remarkably little trace.** The metallic thermal protection
system, chosen for durability and turnaround rather than for mass, has not become standard. The vehicle
health management work and the rapid-turnaround ground operations concepts have not obviously propagated.

**The reason is structural rather than accidental.** Operability improvements pay off across a high flight
rate, and the flight rate that would justify them has not existed.
**A technology whose value depends on a market that does not appear is not a failed technology. It is an unexercised one.**

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

### The Single Point of Failure Is a Story, Not an Explanation

**The most common account of the X-33 is that a tank failed and a programme died, and this article has spent considerable effort arguing against that reading while relying on the same tank.**
The distinction is worth stating carefully.

**The tank did not fail because it was a tank. It failed because of a chain.** The vehicle must land
horizontally, so it is a lifting body, so its cross-section is not circular, so the tank must be conformal,
so it must be lobed, so its walls carry bending, so they are sandwiches, so they have cores, and the core is
the thing that killed it. **Change any link and the failure mode changes.**

**But the chain is an explanation of the mechanism and not of the cancellation**, and conflating the two is
the trap. The arithmetic in the previous section says the programme had a mass problem that the tank failure
did not create and that fixing the tank would not have solved.

### The Counterfactual That Does Not Work

**Suppose the tank had not failed.** The composite tanks would have flown, the vehicle would have made some
number of suborbital flights, and the programme would have declared its technologies demonstrated.
**And VentureStar's hydrogen tanks would still have been 41 percent of its structural allowance**, because
that number comes from the tank's mass, which was known.

**So the failure did not decide anything that the mass had not already decided.** What the failure did was
make the decision unavoidable and public.
**A programme can carry an unfavourable number for years. It cannot carry a photograph of a tank in pieces.**

### Where This Article's Own Framing Is Weakest

**The keystone chosen here is the mass fraction and the tank, and a reader could reasonably choose differently.**
A programme-management reading, in which the cooperative agreement structure and the absence of realistic
cost and risk planning are the subject, is defensible and is
[the reading the Government Accountability Office took when it examined the two cancelled programmes together][ref_gao_x33x34].
**That reading explains the cancellation better than this one does and explains the engineering worse.**

**A second weakness is the treatment of the aerospike.** This article says the engine worked and moves on. A
propulsion-centred treatment would ask what altitude compensation is worth over a real trajectory rather
than at two points, and would have to confront the base-flow behaviour of a truncated plug, which is the
part of the architecture that is genuinely hard and which this article does not attempt.

**A third is that the tank efficiency figure carries the whole verdict.** It rests on a reported tank mass
of 4,600 pounds and a reported capacity of 29,000 gallons. If either is wrong the verdict moves
proportionally. The consistency check below is the only defence available and it is a weak one.

### The Numbers That Hold Each Other Up

**Three figures published separately, and never on the same page, can be checked against one another.** The
tank capacity, the propellant load and the engine mixture ratio imply a fill fraction. The hydrogen load
implied by 210,000 pounds of propellant at a mixture ratio of 5.5 is 14,655 kilograms, which occupies 206.85
cubic metres, against a total tank capacity of 219.55, so

$$\frac{206.85}{219.55} = 0.942$$

**The implied fill is 94.2 percent**, which is what a cryogenic tank actually carries once ullage is allowed
for.

**Had the fill come out above unity, or below three quarters, one of the three published numbers would have been wrong.**
It did not, so the tank mass figure that carries the verdict sits inside a set of numbers that are mutually
consistent. **That is corroboration and not proof, and it is stated as the former.**

## The Contemporary Literature

**The X-33's central problem did not go away when the programme did, and the modern literature on it is larger and more capable than the literature the programme had.**
This section surveys that work. The organising principle is the chain of the article's own argument, so the
subsections run from the tank outward.

### Composite Cryogenic Tanks Since the X-33

**This is the direct descendant of the article's subject and it is an active field.** The problems are the
ones the failure investigation named, and the modern work addresses them directly with barrier films, vented
cores, toughened and nanomodified resin systems, out-of-autoclave processing and automated fibre placement
at scales larger than anything the X-33 attempted.

### Cryogenic Hydrogen Beyond Launch Vehicles

**This is the subsection that would have surprised the programme.** The structural problem of holding liquid
hydrogen in a lightweight conformal vessel is now an aviation problem, a maritime problem and a rail
problem, driven by decarbonisation rather than by launch.
**The X-33's question is being asked again by people who have never heard of it**, and the constraints are
similar enough that the literatures are converging.

## The Source Base

**This article rests on 4,019 references published through 2001, when the programme was cancelled, and 2,186 published from 2015 onward, out of the full set listed below.**

### Both Halves, Counted and Not Only Divided

**A reference pass that reports fractions alone will misdescribe itself, and this one would have misdescribed itself in a way that reads as a regression.**
The primary pass added 1,531 records published through 2001 and 464 from the report literature, taking the
period share from 46.7 percent to 57.7.
**Over the same pass the contemporary count rose, by twenty-four, and the contemporary fraction fell, from 40.6 percent to 31.4.**

**Nothing was removed. The denominator moved.** Saying only that contemporary coverage fell by nine points
would describe a loss that did not occur, and saying only that the period share rose would conceal that the
modern half is now proportionally thinner than it was. Both are given because neither alone is true.

| | Before this pass | After |
|---|---|---|
| Research references cited | 5,324 | 6,966 |
| Period through 2001 | 2,488, 46.7% | 4,019, 57.7% |
| Contemporary 2015 onward | 2,162, 40.6% | 2,186, 31.4% |
| Report literature | 1,231, 23.1% | 1,695, 24.3% |

### What Counts as Primary Here

**A primary source is one contemporary with the work, and for this article the work has an unusually clean boundary.**
The X-33 programme ran from the Phase II award on 2 July 1996 to cancellation in early 2001, and the reports
server holds the programme's own documents from that window in quantity.
**That is the opposite of the previous article's situation and the contrast is measurable.** The X-32 left
exactly one title carrying its designation in a pool of 4,412 harvested records.
**The X-33 pool returns sixty records whose titles carry the designation**, and three harvests later it
still returns sixty, because the vehicle's own documentation was never the thin part.

**The reason is institutional rather than accidental.** A defence competitor is documented by its
manufacturer and its customer, and a National Aeronautics and Space Administration cooperative agreement is
documented by a research agency that publishes.
**The designation is the same in both cases and the documentary consequence is not.**

### The Technology Base Predates the Programme

**A second primary base sits earlier.** The composite structures work, the sandwich mechanics, the
lifting-body aerodynamics and the plug nozzle analysis were largely done in the 1960s through the 1980s. A
1970s report on plug nozzle base pressure is therefore a primary source for this article's propulsion
section in a way that a 2020 computational study is not, and the design-space studies of the period, such as
[Hunt's single-stage-to-orbit design matrix][book_airbreathing_rocket_single_stage_to_orbi], belong to the
same window.

### The Failure Investigation

**The investigation itself is thinly represented in the retrievable record and this is a genuine gap.** The
summary findings are available in secondary and review form and are cited here as such.
**The primary investigation documentation is largely presentation material, and the copies that are retrievable are scanned images from which no text can be extracted.**
That limitation is stated rather than written around.

### What the Equation Pass Did to the Reference Base

**Writing the relations down changed which literature the article needs, and the change was large enough to be worth recording.**
An audit of the twenty-seven subjects the equations actually name found eighteen thin on period coverage and
six at zero,
**including the rocket equation, the ascent loss budget, minimum gauge, integral tank structure, cryopumping and the noncircular pressure vessel.**
None of those was thin because the literature is thin. They were thin because the earlier harvests asked for
tanks, composites and aerospikes,
**and before the equations existed the article had no reason to ask for knockdown factors, face wrinkling or flatwise tension.**

**Two subjects remain genuinely thin after a harvest aimed directly at them, and they are reported rather than padded.**
A search for minimum gauge as a design driver returns nothing in a pool of nearly seven thousand records,
and flatwise tensile testing of a core-to-facing bond, which is the literature of the exact failure that
ended the programme, returns almost nothing retrievable. **The second is the more troubling**, because the
mechanism is well understood and the test is a standard one, so the absence is more likely an artefact of
what is indexed than a gap in what was done.

### The Weakest Link in the Source Chain

**The claim that the aluminium-lithium replacement tank weighed less than the composite tank rests on secondary sources**,
and the article flags it at the point of use as well as here. It is consistent with the derivation and with
the reported role of the joints,
**but consistency with a derivation is not evidence, and a result that agrees with one's own analysis deserves more scepticism rather than less.**

### The Period Base in Full

**Every record harvested for this article is cited, and the ones the argument did not reach individually are listed here by subject rather than discarded.**
A harvested source that is never cited is work done and thrown away, and the sections above draw on the
curated front of each subject while the body of it sits below.

**These are the period records, meaning everything published before 2015.** The contemporary half is listed
in the section above.
